title: Flipped polarity: たい, potential and そう
summary: In 〜が食べたい the main carriage is the thing that makes you want it. With no such thing in the sentence, the feeling flips back to the person.

blocks.text: Every sentence has an **engine** and a **が main carriage**. Everything else tells you more about one of the two. Now look at クレープが食べたい. The carriage is **クレープ**, not "I". The engine is the helper adjective **たい**, so the sentence describes the crepes as having a quality: they stir up the wish to eat them. English puts an ego in the center ("I want"); Japanese is happy to put the thing that causes the feeling in the center.
Polarity flips when the cause is missing

Feelings can be described from the **inducer** (the crepes that stir the wish) or from the **experiencer** (the person who feels it). Japanese treats the two as halves of one event, so the default points at the inducer, but when no inducer is in the sentence the feeling swings to the person. In 東京に行きたい, 東京 already has に and 行く is a verb, so the only possible carriage is a zero: **(私が)** 東京に行きたい.
クレープが食べたい。 Crepes are eat-wanting (to me).
（私が）東京に行きたい。 (I) want to go to Tokyo.
The same flip in the potential

本が読める really says "the book does readable". The carriage is the book. But 私が読める or さくらが読める (no particular thing to read) points at the person: "I can read, I am literate". When no object is the focus, the polarity flips to the doer.

不思議そう on its own would mean "seems mysterious", but mysterious is already a feeling. In 不思議そうに言った it flips to the person: "said in a puzzled way". It describes someone who senses mystery in something.

blocks.jp: お腹が空いた。早く食べたい。
あのケーキが食べたい。
blocks.en: That cake makes (me) want to eat it.
(I) can read this kanji. (the kanji does readable)

blocks.jp: 子供は不思議そうに空を見た。
blocks.en: The child looked at the sky with a puzzled look.

items: In **Aが + 〜たい**, the thing wanted is the carriage and たい is an adjective engine.
With no inducer in the sentence, the feeling or ability points to the **person** (a zero carriage).
The potential and **〜そう** flip in the same way.
Never read が as marking an object; it only ever marks the main carriage.

questions.instruction: In this course, the "main carriage" is the thing the engine (the last verb or adjective) is about. Which word is the main carriage?
questions.prompt: 冷たいジュースが飲みたい。
questions.note: The thing that stirs the wish is the carriage; たい is the engine.
questions.en: I want to drink some cold juice.

questions.instruction: Which word is the engine?
questions.prompt: あの青い車が買いたい。
questions.note: たい makes the verb stem into an adjective engine: 買いたい.
questions.en: I want to buy that blue car.

questions.instruction: Who feels the wish?
questions.note: No inducer is in the sentence, so the feeling points at the person: (私が).
questions.en: I want to go to Japan next year.

questions.instruction: In this course, が marks only the main carriage (the thing the engine is about), not an object. True or false?
questions.prompt: パンが食べたい。 Here が marks the object of 食べる.
questions.note: が only marks the main carriage: the bread is the carriage, 食べたい is the adjective engine.

questions.instruction: Which sentence names the thing that causes the wish?
questions.note: ピザが is the inducer and the carriage; the others have a zero carriage.

questions.instruction: In this course, the main carriage is the thing the engine (the last verb or adjective) is about. A potential verb is self-move: the thing that becomes possible is its carriage. Which word is the main carriage?
questions.note: Like 本が読める, the song "does singable": the song is the carriage.

questions.instruction: When no object is the focus, the potential points to...
options: the person who can do it
questions.note: With no thing in focus, the polarity flips to the doer: "I am literate".

questions.instruction: In 心配そうに見た, who senses the worry?
questions.prompt: お母さんは心配そうに私を見た。
questions.note: 〜そうに flips to the person who senses something: Mom looks worried.
questions.en: Mom looked at me with a worried look.

questions.instruction: Tap the engine
questions.note: 読みたい is the adjective engine; 本 is the carriage.
questions.en: On rainy days I want to read a book.

questions.instruction: Tap the word that shows how the teacher seemed
questions.note: 〜そうに describes the look of a person sensing something.
questions.en: The teacher talked as if enjoying it.

questions.instruction: Tap the carriage (the thing that stirs the wish)
questions.note: 水が is the inducer; 冷たい only describes it.
questions.en: It's hot, so I want some cold water.

questions.instruction: Build the sentence
questions.note: The describer comes first, then the carriage, then the engine.

questions.instruction: Build the sentence
questions.prompt: I can read a Japanese newspaper.
questions.note: 新聞 is the carriage of the potential 読める.

questions.instruction: Build the sentence
questions.note: 楽しそうに tells how she seemed; the engine comes last.
questions.en: The girl sang happily, as if she was having fun.

questions.instruction: Build the sentence
questions.prompt: I want to go to a university in Tokyo.
questions.note: A zero (私が) carriage: に and の are only modifiers.
questions.en: I want to go to a university in Tokyo.

questions.instruction: In this course, the "carriage" is the thing the engine (the last word) is about. Why is クレープが食べたい explained as "crepes are eat-wanting"?
options: たい is an adjective whose carriage is the crepes
questions.note: たい is a helper adjective, and its が carriage is the thing that stirs the wish.

questions.instruction: Which sentence has no が noun, so its main carriage is a hidden 私が?
questions.note: Only 帰りたい has no inducer, so the feeling points at the person.

questions.instruction: Fill the gap
questions.prompt: あの人はいつも楽しそう＿＿歌う。
questions.note: 〜そうに turns the feeling into a way of doing the action.
questions.en: That person always sings as if having fun.

questions.instruction: In this course, a potential verb is self-move: the が noun is its main carriage. True or false?
questions.prompt: 日本語が話せる。 日本語 is the main carriage.
questions.note: The potential is self-move: Japanese "does speakable".

questions.instruction: What kind of word is たい?
questions.note: たい behaves like an い-adjective (たかった, たくない).

questions.instruction: What does 〜そうに describe?
options: How someone looks as they sense something
questions.note: 〜そう flips to the person who senses the feeling.

questions.instruction: Why does 家に帰りたい need a zero carriage?
options: に already marks 家 and 帰る is a verb, so the only carriage left is a zero
が is not allowed with たい
questions.note: Nothing in the sentence can be the carriage, so (私が) is understood.
